claim: Many elongation factors (EFs) crosslink to RNA emerging from transcribing Pol II in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Here we show that many EFs crosslink to RNA emerging from transcribing Pol II in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by PAR-CLIP experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Most EFs crosslink preferentially to mRNAs, rather than unstable non-coding RNAs.
source: Most EFs crosslink preferentially to mRNAs, rather than unstable non-coding RNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data comparing mRNA and CUT binding shown in Figure 4.

claim: RNA contributes to chromatin association of many EFs, including the Pol II serine 2 kinases Ctk1 and Bur1 and the histone H3 methyltransferases Set1 and Set2.
source: RNA contributes to chromatin association of many EFs, including the Pol II serine 2 kinases Ctk1 and Bur1 and the histone H3 methyltransferases Set1 and Set2.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNase treatment experiments shown in Figure 5 demonstrating RNA-dependent chromatin association.

claim: The Ctk1 kinase complex binds RNA in vitro.
source: The Ctk1 kinase complex binds RNA in vitro, consistent with direct EF-RNA interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy experiments with purified CTDK-I complex shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Set1 recruitment to genes in vivo depends on its RNA recognition motifs (RRMs).
source: Set1 recruitment to genes in vivo depends on its RNA recognition motifs (RRMs).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data comparing full-length Set1 with ΔRRM-Set1 shown in Figure 8.

claim: For 12 of 14 EFs tested, PAR-CLIP signals were more than two-fold above background.
source: For 12 of these 14 EFs we obtained PAR-CLIP signals that were more than two-fold above background, showing that these EFs interact with RNA in vivo (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data shown in Figure 1 comparing EF signals to TFIIB background.

claim: Between 42,000 and 520,000 high-confidence protein-RNA crosslinking sites per factor were obtained with p-values below 0.005.
source: We obtained between 42,000 and 520,000 high-confidence protein-RNA crosslinking sites per factor with p-values below 0.005 (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by the data in Table 1.

claim: Spt5, Set1, Ctk1, Spt6, Ctk2 and Bur1 showed high PAR-CLIP signals (>4 fold enrichment over background).
source: Spt5, Set1, Ctk1, Spt6, Ctk2 and Bur1 showed high PAR-CLIP signals (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the fold enrichment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: EFs with moderate PAR-CLIP signals included Rtf1, Ctr9, Cdc73, Bur2, Set2 and Dot1.
source: EFs with moderate signals included Rtf1, Ctr9, Cdc73, Bur2, Set2 and Dot1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fold enrichment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Only the Paf1C subunits Rtf1, Cdc73 and Ctr9 bound RNA according to PAR-CLIP results.
source: For instance, only the Paf1C subunits Rtf1, Cdc73 and Ctr9 bound RNA according to the PAR-CLIP results, and the same subunits bound radioactively labeled RNA after immunoprecipitation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data and radioactive RNA co-precipitation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Normalization of PAR-CLIP data is crucial to enable comparison of PAR-CLIP signals between individual transcripts and transcript classes.
source: Briefly, the raw PAR-CLIP signal is proportional to the occupancy of the factor on RNA and to the concentration of RNAs covering the U site. Therefore, normalization is crucial to enable comparison of PAR-CLIP signals between individual transcripts and transcript classes.
evidence: This is a methodological claim based on the principles of PAR-CLIP data analysis, supported by previous work (Baejen et al., 2014).

claim: PAR-CLIP occupancies were high at the 5′-end of mRNAs and decreased shortly before the pA site, with few exceptions.
source: Generally, PAR-CLIP occupancies were high at the 5′-end of mRNAs and decreased shortly before the pA site, with few exceptions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the metagene profiles shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Set2 and Dot1 showed more RNA-binding sites over transcript bodies.
source: First, the histone methyltransferases Set2 and Dot1, for which the corresponding methylation marks accumulate in gene bodies (Bannister et al., 2005; Pokholok et al., 2005), showed more RNA-binding sites over transcript bodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data in Figure 3A and cited literature on histone methylation patterns.

claim: Set1 crosslinked to mRNAs mainly near the beginning of transcripts.
source: Second, Set1 crosslinked to mRNAs mainly near the beginning of transcripts, which was expected since Set1 and its methylation mark, H3K4me3, are observed in promoter-proximal regions of genes (Ng et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data in Figure 3A and cited literature on Set1 localization.

claim: The kinases Ctk1 and Bur1 and their cyclin partners Ctk2 and Bur2 were enriched near the 5′-end but also in the transcript body.
source: Third, the kinases Ctk1 and Bur1 and their cyclin partners Ctk2 and Bur2 were enriched near the 5′-end but also in the transcript body.
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 5′-peak for Bur1-Bur2 slightly preceded that of Ctk1-Ctk2.
source: The 5′-peak for Bur1-Bur2 slightly preceded that of Ctk1-Ctk2.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of PAR-CLIP profiles in Figure 3A.

claim: All EFs cross-linked to introns.
source: All EFs cross-linked to introns (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating that they bind pre-mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data on introns shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All EFs showed positive processing indices (PIs), indicating binding to pre-mRNA.
source: All EFs showed positive PIs, indicating binding to pre-mRNA, in contrast to the negative PIs that we previously obtained for typical RNA binders of processed, mature mRNA, such as Pab1 and Pub1 (Figure 3B) (Baejen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by processing index calculations shown in Figure 3B and comparison with previously published data.

claim: Spt5 colocalizes with the Cbc2 subunit of the cap-binding complex.
source: We found that Spt5 colocalizes with the Cbc2 subunit of the cap-binding complex, consistent with its recruitment during early elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both Ctk1 and Bur1 colocalized with binding sites of Set1 and splicing factors.
source: Both Ctk1 and Bur1 colocalized with binding sites of Set1 and splicing factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Paf1C subunits colocalized with Set2.
source: Paf1C subunits colocalized with Set2, whereas RNA 3′-processing and surveillance factors formed separate groups (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Spt5 was equally distributed between CUTs and mRNAs.
source: This revealed that EFs bind to these transcript classes with distinct preferences. Spt5 was equally distributed between CUTs and mRNAs whereas Set1 preferentially bound mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data comparing mRNA and CUT binding shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Set1 preferentially bound mRNAs compared to CUTs.
source: Spt5 was equally distributed between CUTs and mRNAs whereas Set1 preferentially bound mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data comparing mRNA and CUT binding shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All other EFs (besides Spt5 and Set1) were depleted at CUTs relative to their mRNA occupancies.
source: All other EFs were depleted at CUTs relative to their mRNA occupancies (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data comparing mRNA and CUT binding shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Motif analysis around the strongest PAR-CLIP sites for each EF did not find any significantly enriched motifs, indicating that EFs bind RNA in a non-specific manner.
source: We carried out motif analysis around the strongest PAR-CLIP sites for each EF using XXmotif (Luehr et al., 2012) and could not find any significantly enriched motifs, indicating that EFs bind RNA in a non-specific manner.
evidence: This claim is based on computational motif analysis of PAR-CLIP data.

claim: RNase treatment strongly decreased the levels of chromatin-associated enzymes Set1, Set2, Dot1, Bur1, Ctk1, and the cyclins Bur2 and Ctk2.
source: We found that RNase treatment strongly decreased the levels of chromatin-associated enzymes Set1, Set2, Dot1, Bur1, Ctk1, and the cyclins Bur2 and Ctk2 (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis after RNase treatment shown in Figure 5.

claim: Rtf1 was partially lost upon RNase treatment.
source: With respect to Paf1C, Rtf1 was partially lost upon RNase treatment, whereas Leo1 and Paf1 were not significantly affected (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis after RNase treatment shown in Figure 5.

claim: Leo1 and Paf1 were not significantly affected by RNase treatment.
source: With respect to Paf1C, Rtf1 was partially lost upon RNase treatment, whereas Leo1 and Paf1 were not significantly affected (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis after RNase treatment shown in Figure 5.

claim: Spt5 binding to chromatin depended on RNA.
source: Spt5 binding to chromatin also depended on RNA, whereas Spt6 was not significantly affected by RNase treatment (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis after RNase treatment shown in Figure 5.

claim: Spt6 was not significantly affected by RNase treatment.
source: Spt5 binding to chromatin also depended on RNA, whereas Spt6 was not significantly affected by RNase treatment (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis after RNase treatment shown in Figure 5.

claim: RNase treatment did not affect association of Pol II with chromatin.
source: Also as expected, RNase treatment did not affect association of Pol II with chromatin, showing that the observed losses of EFs from chromatin upon RNase treatment were not due to a loss of Pol II (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis after RNase treatment shown in Figure 5.

claim: RNase treatment did not affect TFIIB chromatin binding.
source: As a negative control, we subjected TFIIB to the RNase assay. We observed no differences in chromatin binding after RNase treatment (Figure 5), consistent with recruitment of TFIIB to DNA during transcription initiation (Sainsbury et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis after RNase treatment shown in Figure 5 and cited literature on TFIIB function.

claim: Purified CTDK-I complex was active and phosphorylated GST-CTD at the Ser2 position in vitro.
source: Both the GST-CTD and the Rpb1 subunit of Pol II were readily phosphorylated by CTDK-I at the Ser2 position in vitro (Figure 6B,C), showing that our purified CTDK-I complex was active.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Purified CTDK-I complex phosphorylated the Rpb1 subunit of Pol II at the Ser2 position in vitro.
source: Both the GST-CTD and the Rpb1 subunit of Pol II were readily phosphorylated by CTDK-I at the Ser2 position in vitro (Figure 6B,C), showing that our purified CTDK-I complex was active.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: CTDK-I bound ssRNAs with 45% or 24% GC content with similar affinities.
source: CTDK-I bound both ssRNAs with similar affinities (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: CTDK-I showed some preference for U-rich RNA over A-rich RNA.
source: We also tested U- or A-rich sequences for association with CTDK-I and found some preference for U-rich RNA (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy experiments shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: CTDK-I bound to duplex DNA much more weakly than to ssRNA.
source: Consistent with this, CTDK-I bound to duplex DNA much more weakly (dsDNA, Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CTDK-I binds to single-stranded RNA with apparent Kd values in the nanomolar range.
source: Fitting the data with binding curves by linear regression resulted in apparent Kd's in the nanomolar range (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: EFs interacted with RNA already from around 20 nt downstream of the capped 5′-end of mRNAs.
source: In contrast, PAR-CLIP results showed that EFs interacted with RNA already from around 20 nt downstream of the capped 5′-end of mRNAs (Figure 7, blue lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of PAR-CLIP and ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7.

claim: EF occupancy increased within 100–600 bp downstream of the TSS according to ChIP-Seq data.
source: Metagene analysis of our ChIP-Seq data revealed that EF occupancy increased within 100–600 bp downstream of the TSS, and was generally high in gene bodies (Figure 7, red lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq metagene analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Set2 occupies transcripts at the 5′-end but showed peak levels of genome association only in the downstream region, with peak levels 450–300 bp upstream of the pA site.
source: This difference was most pronounced for Set2, which occupies transcripts at the 5′-end but showed peak levels of genome association only in the downstream region, with peak levels 450–300 bp upstream of the pA site.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of PAR-CLIP and ChIP-Seq data for Set2 shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the direction of transcription, the PAR-CLIP signals for methyltransferases increased first, followed by an onset of ChIP-Seq signals for the respective histone methylation marks, which in turn preceded the increase in ChIP-Seq signals for the enzymes.
source: In the direction of transcription, the PAR-CLIP signals for methyltransferases increased first, followed by an onset of ChIP-Seq signals for the respective histone methylation marks, which in turn preceded the increase in ChIP-Seq signals for the enzymes (Figure 7, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of PAR-CLIP, histone mark ChIP-Seq, and enzyme ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Gene regions within the first 1000 bp downstream of the TSS showed a severe decrease in ΔRRM-Set1 occupancy.
source: Gene regions within the first 1000 bp downstream of the TSS showed a severe decrease in ΔRRM-Set1 occupancy (Figure 8C; genomic regions 1, 2, 4 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data comparing full-length Set1 with ΔRRM-Set1 shown in Figure 8C.

claim: A decrease in Set1 occupancy was detected in the absence of Paf1, confirming the role of Paf1C in Set1 recruitment.
source: Similarly, we also detected a decrease in Set1 occupancy in the absence of Paf1, confirming the role of Paf1C in Set1 recruitment (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data in ΔPaf1 strain shown in Figure 8C and cited literature on Paf1C function.

claim: Set1 contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) at residues 247–375 and 376–579.
source: To test the model of RNA-based recruitment for a particular factor, we investigated whether Set1 gene occupancy depends on the N-terminal region of the protein that contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRMs, residues 247–375 and 376–579) that bind RNA in vitro (Trésaugues et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature describing Set1 structure and RNA binding.

claim: Set1 RRMs bind RNA in vitro.
source: To test the model of RNA-based recruitment for a particular factor, we investigated whether Set1 gene occupancy depends on the N-terminal region of the protein that contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRMs, residues 247–375 and 376–579) that bind RNA in vitro (Trésaugues et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Spt5 binds RNA in vitro.
source: Spt5 and Set1 bind RNA in vitro (Meyer et al., 2015; Missra and Gilmour, 2010; Trésaugues et al., 2006; Halbach et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Ctk1 and Bur1 in vivo occupancy at active genes depends on the cap-binding complex.
source: Ctk1 and Bur1 in vivo occupancy at active genes depends on the cap-binding complex, which binds 5′-capped RNA (Hossain et al., 2013; Lidschreiber et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Paf1C binds RNA, which is required for full gene occupancy.
source: Paf1C binds RNA, which is required for full gene occupancy (Dermody and Buratowski, 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Spt5 binds the body of the Pol II elongation complex.
source: Spt5 binds the body of the Pol II elongation complex (Grohmann et al., 2011; Klein et al., 2011; Martinez-Rucobo et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Bur1, Spt6 and Set2 bind the CTD.
source: Bur1, Spt6 and Set2 bind the CTD (Dengl et al., 2009; Kizer et al., 2005; Li et al., 2003; Phatnani et al., 2004; Sun et al., 2010; Yoh et al., 2007; Qiu et al., 2009; Li et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Interaction of Paf1C with Pol II involves Spt5.
source: Interaction of Paf1C with Pol II involves Spt5 (Liu et al., 2009; Mayekar et al., 2013; Wier et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2009; Qiu et al., 2012, 2009) and the CTD (Qiu et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Interaction of Set1 with Pol II involves Paf1C.
source: whereas interaction of Set1 with Pol II involves Paf1C (Krogan et al., 2003a; Ng et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Mutations in EFs that prevent their polymerase interactions do not abolish gene occupancy of such factors, including Bur1, Paf1C subunits, Spt6, and Set2.
source: However, other recruitment mechanisms exist because mutations in EFs that prevent their polymerase interactions do not abolish gene occupancy of such factors, including Bur1, Paf1C subunits, Spt6, and Set2 (Ng et al., 2003; Qiu et al., 2012, 2009; Mayer et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2009; Krogan et al., 2003b).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Ctk1 is the yeast CTD serine 2 (Ser2) kinase.
source: Further, it remains unknown how the yeast CTD serine 2 (Ser2) kinase Ctk1 is recruited
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ctk1 function.

claim: Spt6 and Set2 bind the Ser2-phosphorylated CTD.
source: which is apparently a prerequisite for recruitment of Spt6 and Set2, because these factors bind the Ser2-phosphorylated CTD (Dengl et al., 2009; Kizer et al., 2005; Li et al., 2003; Phatnani et al., 2004; Sun et al., 2010; Yoh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: RNA processing factors are recruited during Pol II elongation for co-transcriptional capping, splicing, and 3′-processing of the pre-mRNA.
source: Such RNA interactions are well established for RNA processing factors that are recruited during Pol II elongation (Perales and Bentley, 2009; Bentley, 2005; Baejen et al., 2014; Tuck and Tollervey, 2013) for co-transcriptional capping (Martinez-Rucobo et al., 2015), splicing (Bentley, 2005; Saldi et al., 2016), and 3′-processing (Proudfoot, 2011; Shi and Manley, 2015) of the pre-mRNA.
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: TFIIH phosphorylates Ser5 residues in the CTD during transcription initiation.
source: When the initiation complex assembles at the promoter, TFIIH phosphorylates Ser5 residues in the CTD and this enables recruitment of the capping enzyme (Cho et al., 1997; Fabrega et al., 2003; Rodriguez et al., 2000; Schroeder et al., 2000; Schwer and Shuman, 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Ser5 phosphorylation enables recruitment of the capping enzyme.
source: When the initiation complex assembles at the promoter, TFIIH phosphorylates Ser5 residues in the CTD and this enables recruitment of the capping enzyme (Cho et al., 1997; Fabrega et al., 2003; Rodriguez et al., 2000; Schroeder et al., 2000; Schwer and Shuman, 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Ser5 phosphorylation is needed for high gene occupancy with some EFs.
source: The requirement for a cap on RNA befits the observation that Ser5 phosphorylation is needed for high gene occupancy with some EFs (Qiu et al., 2012, 2009, 2006; Ng et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Nascent RNA contributes to EF recruitment to transcribing Pol II.
source: These results strongly suggest that nascent RNA contributes to EF recruitment to transcribing Pol II.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: EF-RNA interactions facilitate assembly of the elongation complex on transcribed genes when RNA emerges from Pol II.
source: We propose that EF-RNA interactions facilitate assembly of the elongation complex on transcribed genes when RNA emerges from Pol II, and that loss of EF-RNA interactions upon RNA cleavage at the polyadenylation site triggers disassembly of the elongation complex.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Loss of EF-RNA interactions upon RNA cleavage at the polyadenylation site triggers disassembly of the elongation complex.
source: We propose that EF-RNA interactions facilitate assembly of the elongation complex on transcribed genes when RNA emerges from Pol II, and that loss of EF-RNA interactions upon RNA cleavage at the polyadenylation site triggers disassembly of the elongation complex.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The transcribing Pol II complex may be viewed as a self-organizing system that is encoded in the DNA, but only realized on the level of RNA.
source: Thus, the transcribing Pol II complex may be viewed as a self-organizing system that is encoded in the DNA, but only realized on the level of RNA, which plays crucial roles in complex assembly and disassembly.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the findings.

claim: RNA plays crucial roles in elongation complex assembly and disassembly.
source: Thus, the transcribing Pol II complex may be viewed as a self-organizing system that is encoded in the DNA, but only realized on the level of RNA, which plays crucial roles in complex assembly and disassembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: RNA-based recruitment of EFs provides a missing link in understanding how the transcription cycle is coordinated.
source: Finally, we predict that RNA-based recruitment of EFs provides a missing link in our understanding of how the transcription cycle is coordinated.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings.

claim: Binding of Nrd1 to CUTs might hinder RNA binding of some EFs.
source: Binding of Nrd1 to CUTs might hinder RNA binding of some EFs, especially those which possess lower RNA binding affinity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the differential binding of EFs to CUTs versus mRNAs.

claim: Nrd1 selectively binds to CUTs.
source: CUTs are rapidly degraded by a surveillance system, which includes Nrd1 (Schulz et al., 2013; Vasiljeva et al., 2008; Steinmetz and Brow, 1996). Nrd1 selectively binds to CUTs (Figure 4C) via motifs that are enriched in CUTs compared to mRNAs (Schulz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by PAR-CLIP data shown in Figure 4C and cited literature.

claim: Motifs recognized by Nrd1 are enriched in CUTs compared to mRNAs.
source: Nrd1 selectively binds to CUTs (Figure 4C) via motifs that are enriched in CUTs compared to mRNAs (Schulz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: The obtained PAR-CLIP data sets were highly reproducible.
source: The obtained data sets were highly reproducible (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by replicate correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The obtained ChIP-Seq data sets were highly reproducible.
source: The obtained ChIP-Seq data sets were highly reproducible (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by replicate correlation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only ~4% of yeast genes contain introns.
source: However, only ~4% of yeast genes contain introns (Qin et al., 2016), preventing general statements related to all pre-mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Splicing generally occurs co-transcriptionally.
source: Taking into account that splicing generally occurs co-transcriptionally (Kornblihtt et al., 2004; Tennyson et al., 1995; Listerman et al., 2006), our data show that EFs interact with nascent pre-mRNA.
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: CUTs often arise from upstream antisense transcription of bidirectional promoters.
source: We next analyzed our PAR-CLIP data for EF binding to non-coding Pol II transcripts including short-lived cryptic unstable transcripts (CUTs), which often arise from upstream antisense transcription of bidirectional promoters (Wyers et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: CTDK-I is the main yeast kinase responsible for phosphorylating the Pol II CTD at Ser2.
source: CTDK-I is the main yeast kinase responsible for phosphorylating the Pol II CTD at Ser2 (Patturajan et al., 1999; Cho et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD at Ser2 is a decisive event in establishing a mature Pol II elongation complex.
source: CTDK-I is the main yeast kinase responsible for phosphorylating the Pol II CTD at Ser2 (Patturajan et al., 1999; Cho et al., 2001), and this is a decisive event in establishing a mature Pol II elongation complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of Ser2 phosphorylation.

claim: The Yra1 RRM domain binds both RNA and the phosphorylated CTD.
source: However, the same domain can mediate both RNA and protein interactions, as documented for the RNA export factor Yra1, which contains a RNA recognition motif (RRM) domain that binds both RNA and the phosphorylated CTD (MacKellar and Greenleaf, 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Set2 contains a SRI domain that binds the phosphorylated CTD.
source: Set2 contains a SRI domain that binds the phosphorylated CTD (Dengl et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2010; Yoh et al., 2007; MacKellar and Greenleaf, 2011), but may also bind RNA.
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: The three Paf1C subunits that bind RNA in vivo (Cdc73, Ctr9 and Rtf1) also interact with the phosphorylated CTD and the phosphorylated C-terminal region (CTR) of Spt5 in vitro.
source: The three Paf1C subunits that bind RNA in vivo, namely Cdc73, Ctr9 and Rtf1, also interact with the phosphorylated CTD and the phosphorylated C-terminal region (CTR) of Spt5 in vitro (Qiu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Rtf1 contains a positively charged Plus-3 domain that binds the phosphorylated CTR.
source: Rtf1 contains a positively charged Plus-3 domain (Finn et al., 2014) that binds the phosphorylated CTR (Wier et al., 2013) and single-stranded nucleic acids (de Jong et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: The Rtf1 Plus-3 domain binds single-stranded nucleic acids.
source: Rtf1 contains a positively charged Plus-3 domain (Finn et al., 2014) that binds the phosphorylated CTR (Wier et al., 2013) and single-stranded nucleic acids (de Jong et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Many EFs contain domains that can interact with RNA or with the phosphorylated CTD or CTR.
source: We predict that many EFs contain domains that can interact with RNA or with the phosphorylated CTD or CTR, which resemble RNA in its flexible nature and negative charge.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings and structural considerations.

claim: The phosphorylated CTD and CTR resemble RNA in their flexible nature and negative charge.
source: We predict that many EFs contain domains that can interact with RNA or with the phosphorylated CTD or CTR, which resemble RNA in its flexible nature and negative charge.
evidence: This is a structural/biochemical inference.

claim: For some EFs, binding to RNA or the CTD may be mutually exclusive.
source: Whereas for some EFs binding to RNA or the CTD may be mutually exclusive, others can bind both Pol II and RNA at the same time, for example Spt5.
evidence: This is a speculation about different binding modes.

claim: Some EFs can bind both Pol II and RNA at the same time, for example Spt5.
source: Whereas for some EFs binding to RNA or the CTD may be mutually exclusive, others can bind both Pol II and RNA at the same time, for example Spt5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing Spt5 binds both Pol II and RNA.

claim: Capped RNA could help to recruit EFs.
source: The nascent RNA then receives a 5′-cap (Martinez-Rucobo et al., 2015), and capped RNA could then help to recruit EFs.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the findings.

claim: RNA-based recruitment of the major Ser2 kinase, Ctk1, would lead to CTD phosphorylation on Ser2 residues and stable binding of other EFs.
source: RNA-based recruitment of the major Ser2 kinase, Ctk1, would then lead to CTD phosphorylation on Ser2 residues and stable binding of other EFs.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the findings.

claim: Transcription of a pA site triggers RNA cleavage, which would facilitate loss of many RNA-bound EFs and render the polymerase prone to transcription termination.
source: Eventually, transcription of a pA site triggers RNA cleavage, and this would facilitate loss of many RNA-bound EFs and render the polymerase prone to transcription termination.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the findings.

claim: RNA-based recruitment of Ser2 kinases explains why Ser2 phosphorylation of the CTD is restricted to transcribing polymerases.
source: A model of kinase recruitment by capped RNA predicts that these enzymes are lost from the transcribing enzyme upon RNA cleavage at the pA site, and this is indeed observed by ChIP-Seq. In conclusion, RNA-based recruitment of Ser2 kinases explains why Ser2 phosphorylation of the CTD is restricted to transcribing polymerases, whereas free or initiating polymerases are not phosphorylated at Ser2 residues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and proposed model.

claim: Free or initiating polymerases are not phosphorylated at Ser2 residues.
source: In conclusion, RNA-based recruitment of Ser2 kinases explains why Ser2 phosphorylation of the CTD is restricted to transcribing polymerases, whereas free or initiating polymerases are not phosphorylated at Ser2 residues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CTD phosphorylation patterns.

claim: Set1 recruitment not only depends on the Paf1 complex, but also on binding to nascent RNA.
source: These results indicate that Set1 recruitment not only depends on the Paf1 complex, but also on binding to nascent RNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP-qPCR experiments comparing Set1-TAP, ΔRRM-Set1-TAP, and ΔPaf1 Set1-TAP strains.

claim: Interactions of EFs with nascent RNA contribute to EF recruitment to actively transcribed genes in vivo.
source: Taken together, several lines of evidence presented here strongly suggest that interactions of EFs with nascent RNA contribute to EF recruitment to actively transcribed genes in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.
